sections.title: Numerical Type
marking: Marking not printed in the paper; JEE Advanced default assumed:

concepts: Intersection of two lines in 3D and foot of perpendicular from a point to a line
questions.question: Let $L_1:\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-1}{-1}=\dfrac{z+1}{0}$ and $L_2:\dfrac{x-2}{2}=\dfrac{y}{0}=\dfrac{z+4}{\alpha}$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, be two lines which intersect at the point $B$. If $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A(1,1,-1)$ on $L_2$, then the value of $26\alpha(PB)^2$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Equate the two parametrisations to get $B$ and $\alpha$; then $P$ is found from $\overrightarrow{AP}\perp L_2$.
solution: A point of $L_1$ is $(3\lambda+1,\,-\lambda+1,\,-1)$ and a point of $L_2$ is $(2\mu+2,\,0,\,\alpha\mu-4)$.
At the common point $B$ these are equal: $3\lambda+1=2\mu+2$, $-\lambda+1=0$ and $-1=\alpha\mu-4$.
Let $P=(2\delta+2,\,0,\,3\delta-4)$ on $L_2$ (here $\alpha=3$, direction ratios of $L_2$ are $2,0,3$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the first equation as 3*lambda+1 = 2*lambda+2; it should be 3*lambda+1 = 2*mu+2 (mu, not lambda, is the parameter of L2). The values lambda=mu=1, alpha=3 and the answer 216 are unchanged. The step giving delta = 7/13 (from 2(2d+1)+3(3d-3)=0) and the value PB^2 = 36/13 were not shown; added.

alternate_solutions.idea: $PB$ is the length of the projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $L_2$, so $P$ never has to be found.
solution: As before, $B(4,0,-1)$ and $\alpha=3$; the direction of $L_2$ is $\vec d=(2,0,3)$, $|\vec d|^2=13$.
$P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ on $L_2$, and $B$ lies on $L_2$; so $PB$ is the component of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ along $L_2$.

useful_results: If $B$ is any point of a line with direction $\vec d$ and $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$, then $PB=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ and $AP^2=AB^2-PB^2$ (Pythagoras in $\triangle APB$).

Two lines $\frac{x-x_1}{a_1}=\dots$ and $\frac{x-x_2}{a_2}=\dots$ intersect iff the parametrised coordinates can be equated: three equations in two parameters, so a parameter such as $\alpha$ here is fixed by the consistency (coplanarity) condition.
A line with a zero direction ratio, e.g. $\frac{z+1}{0}$, lies in the plane $z=-1$ (the zero fixes that coordinate); this removes one unknown at once.

concepts: Area of a triangle using the cross product of vectors
questions.question: Let $ABC$ be a triangle of area $15\sqrt2$ and the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}=\hat i+2\hat j-7\hat k$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=6\hat i+d\hat j-2\hat k$, $d>0$. Then the square of the length of the largest side of the triangle $ABC$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$ gives a quadratic in $d$; then compare the three squared sides.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at AB=sqrt54, AC=sqrt44, BC=sqrt(25+0+25) without evaluating BC^2 = 50, comparing the three squares or stating the answer 54, and does not say that the root d = -2/5 is rejected because d>0. Added these steps; no value was wrong.

alternate_solutions.idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$ gives the quadratic in $d$ without a cross product.
solution: Then $AC^2=44$ and $BC^2=|\overrightarrow{AC}-\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=44+54-2(24)=50$, so the largest square is $54$.

useful_results: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$ (Lagrange): the area of a triangle needs only dot products, no components of a cross product.

Area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$; with $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}-\overrightarrow{AB}$ one gets $BC^2=AB^2+AC^2-2\,\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}$.
In a triangle the longest side is opposite the largest angle; here $AB^2=54>BC^2=50>AC^2=44$, i.e. the largest side is opposite the angle at $C$.

concepts: Vector triple product and cross-product equations
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k$ and a vector $\vec c$ be such that $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)+\vec b\times\vec c=\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$, then $\left(24-\vec b\cdot\vec c\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Cross the given relation with $\vec a$ to expand the triple products, then dot with $\vec b$ so only $\vec b\cdot\vec c$ survives.
solution: Expanding, $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c=(1,8,13)$.
Take $\vec a\times$ both sides: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)+\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec c)+\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec a\times(\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k)$.

Using $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z$: $(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a-a^2\vec b+(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a-a^2\vec c+(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.
Here $\vec a\cdot\vec b=6-12-20=-26$, $a^2=29$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$, so this is $-26\vec a-29\vec b+13\vec a-29\vec c+13\vec b+26\vec c$.
That simplifies to $-13\vec a-16\vec b-3\vec c=\vec a\times(\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k)$.
Dot with $\vec b$: $-13\,\vec a\cdot\vec b-16b^2-3\,\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec a\times(\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k)\cdot\vec b$.
The right side is a triple product, $\left|\begin{matrix}2&-3&4\\1&8&13\\3&4&-5\end{matrix}\right|=-396$, and $b^2=50$.
Hence $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-22$ and $24-\vec b\cdot\vec c=46$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $\vec c$ itself: $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c$ is known, so $\vec c=\vec c_0+t(\vec a+\vec b)$ with $t$ fixed by $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$.
solution: Write $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b=(5,1,-1)$. The relation is $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ with $\vec w=(1,8,13)-\vec a\times\vec b$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=(-1,22,17)$, so $\vec w=(2,-14,-4)$; note $\vec s\cdot\vec w=10-14+4=0$, as it must be.

$\vec s\times(\vec w\times\vec s)=|\vec s|^2\vec w-\vec s(\vec s\cdot\vec w)=|\vec s|^2\vec w$, so a particular solution is $\vec c_0=\dfrac{\vec w\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}=\dfrac{(18,-18,72)}{27}=\left(\frac23,-\frac23,\frac83\right)$.
The general solution is $\vec c=\vec c_0+t\vec s$ (adding a multiple of $\vec s$ does not change $\vec s\times\vec c$).
$\vec a\cdot\vec c_0=\frac{4+6+32}{3}=14$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec s=3$, so $14+3t=13\Rightarrow t=-\frac13$.

useful_results: $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ is solvable only if $\vec s\cdot\vec w=0$, and then $\vec c=\dfrac{\vec w\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}+t\vec s$: the solution is a line parallel to $\vec s$; one more scalar condition fixes $t$.

$\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z$; crossing a relation with a known vector and then dotting with a well-chosen vector eliminates unwanted unknowns.
$(\vec u\times\vec v)\cdot\vec b=[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec b]$, a determinant; so $\vec a\times\vec u\cdot\vec b=[\vec a\ \vec u\ \vec b]$.
Sum rule: $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c$ - the cyclic sum of three cross products.

concepts: Vector equation $\vec r\times\vec a=\vec p\times\vec a$ and its general solution
questions.question: Let $\vec a=9\hat i-13\hat j+25\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i+7\hat j-13\hat k$ and $\vec c=17\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k$ be three given vectors. If $\vec r$ is a vector such that $\vec r\times\vec a=(\vec b+\vec c)\times\vec a$ and $\vec r\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0$, then $\dfrac{\left|593\vec r+67\vec a\right|^2}{(593)^2}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\left(\vec r-(\vec b+\vec c)\right)\times\vec a=\vec 0$ means $\vec r=\vec b+\vec c+\lambda\vec a$; the dot condition fixes $\lambda=-\frac{67}{593}$.
solution: $\vec r\times\vec a=(\vec b+\vec c)\times\vec a\Rightarrow\left(\vec r-(\vec b+\vec c)\right)\times\vec a=\vec0$.
So $\vec r-(\vec b+\vec c)$ is parallel to $\vec a$: $\vec r=(\vec b+\vec c)+\lambda\vec a$.
$\vec b+\vec c=20\hat i+5\hat j-12\hat k$, so $\vec r=(20+9\lambda)\hat i+(5-13\lambda)\hat j+(25\lambda-12)\hat k$.
$\vec b-\vec c=-14\hat i+9\hat j-14\hat k$, and $\vec r\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Do not find $\lambda$: show that $\vec w=593\vec r+67\vec a$ and $593(\vec b+\vec c)$ satisfy the same two conditions, which fix the vector uniquely.
solution: Let $\vec s=\vec b+\vec c=(20,5,-12)$, $\vec n=\vec b-\vec c=(-14,9,-14)$ and $\vec w=593\vec r+67\vec a$.
Since $\vec r\times\vec a=\vec s\times\vec a$, $\vec w\times\vec a=593\,\vec s\times\vec a$, so $\vec w-593\vec s$ is parallel to $\vec a$.
$\vec w\cdot\vec n=593(\vec r\cdot\vec n)+67(\vec a\cdot\vec n)=0+67(-593)$, and $593\,\vec s\cdot\vec n=593(-67)$: equal, so $(\vec w-593\vec s)\cdot\vec n=0$.
A vector parallel to $\vec a$ with $(\cdot)\cdot\vec n=0$ must be $\vec 0$ because $\vec a\cdot\vec n=-593\neq0$.
So $\vec w=593\vec s$ and the required value is $|\vec s|^2=400+25+144=569$.

useful_results: $\vec r\times\vec a=\vec p\times\vec a\iff\vec r=\vec p+\lambda\vec a$: the solution set is a line through $\vec p$ parallel to $\vec a$.
Adding one scalar condition such as $\vec r\cdot\vec n=0$ gives $\lambda=-\dfrac{\vec p\cdot\vec n}{\vec a\cdot\vec n}$ (valid when $\vec a\cdot\vec n\neq0$): a line-plane intersection.
$(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=|\vec b|^2-|\vec c|^2$: dot products of sums and differences reduce to squared lengths (here $227-294=-67$).
Instance: the numbers $593$ and $67$ in the question are exactly $-\vec a\cdot\vec n$ and $-\vec s\cdot\vec n$, which signals that the answer is $|\vec b+\vec c|^2$.

concepts: Scalar and vector product of vectors; angle between two vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two vectors such that $|\vec a|=1$, $|\vec b|=4$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$. If $\vec c=(2\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$ and the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $\alpha$, then $192\sin^2\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-3|\vec b|^2$ and $|\vec c|^2$ splits into two orthogonal parts.
solution: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=(2\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b-3|\vec b|^2=-3|\vec b|^2$ (as $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$).
$|\vec b||\vec c|\cos\alpha=-3|\vec b|^2\Rightarrow|\vec c|\cos\alpha=-12$, because $|\vec b|=4$.
$|\vec c|^2=\left|2\vec a\times\vec b-3\vec b\right|^2=64\times\frac34+144=192$ (the cross term vanishes since $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$).

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec c$ has one part along $-\vec b$ and one part $2\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so $|\vec c|\sin\alpha$ is simply the length of the perpendicular part.
solution: $\vec c=-3\vec b+2(\vec a\times\vec b)$ with $2(\vec a\times\vec b)\perp\vec b$: the component of $\vec c$ along $\vec b$ is $-3\vec b$, the perpendicular component is $2\vec a\times\vec b$.
Therefore $|\vec c|\sin\alpha=|2\vec a\times\vec b|$ (perpendicular component) and $|\vec c|\cos\alpha=-3|\vec b|=-12$.
$|\vec c|^2=|-3\vec b|^2+|2\vec a\times\vec b|^2=144+|2\vec a\times\vec b|^2$, and $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=16-4=12$, so $|2\vec a\times\vec b|^2=48$.
$|\vec c|^2=144+48=192$, exactly the number in the question.

useful_results: If $\vec c=p\vec b+\vec q$ with $\vec q\perp\vec b$, then $|\vec c|\cos\alpha=p|\vec b|$ and $|\vec c|\sin\alpha=|\vec q|$ (parallel and perpendicular components).
$\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$; hence $|\vec u+\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec u|^2+|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$ for any $\vec u$ in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$.
Lagrange: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$; here $16-4=12$ without finding the angle.

concepts: Vector product equation and system of linear equations in vector components
questions.question: Let $\vec a=3\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be a vector such that $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)+24\hat j-6\hat k$ and $(\vec a-\vec b+\hat i)\cdot\vec c=-3$. Then $|\vec c|^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Write $\vec c=(x,y,z)$; the cross-product equation gives a rank-2 system, completed by the dot-product equation.
solution: $\vec a+\vec b=5\hat i+\hat j+4\hat k$ and $\vec a\times\vec b=7\hat i-7\hat j-7\hat k$.
So $(5\hat i+\hat j+4\hat k)\times\vec c=2(7\hat i-7\hat j-7\hat k)+24\hat j-6\hat k=14\hat i+10\hat j-20\hat k$.
Let $\vec c=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$. Then $\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\5&1&4\\x&y&z\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i(z-4y)-\hat j(5z-4x)+\hat k(5y-x)$.
$\vec a-\vec b+\hat i=2\hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k$, so $2x+3y-2z=-3$.
From $z=14+4y$ and $x=5y+20$: $4x-5z=20y+80-70-20y=10$ holds identically, so $y$ is free in the first three equations.
Then $x=5$, $z=2$, so $\vec c=5\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 'x=5, y=-3, z=2' straight after the four equations. The cross-product system has rank 2 (the three equations are dependent), so it needs the dot-product equation to fix the vector; the solving steps (x=5y+20, z=14+4y, then 5y+12=-3) were missing and were added. The values and the answer 38 are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split $\vec c$ into a part perpendicular to $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b$, fixed by the cross product, and a multiple of $\vec s$ fixed by the dot product.
solution: Let $\vec s=(5,1,4)$ and $\vec w=(14,10,-20)$; $\vec s\cdot\vec w=70+10-80=0$, so $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ is consistent.
A particular solution is $\vec c_0=\dfrac{\vec w\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}$ with $\vec w\times\vec s=(60,-156,-36)$ and $|\vec s|^2=42$, so $\vec c_0=\frac17(10,-26,-6)$.
Let $\vec m=(2,3,-2)$. $\vec m\cdot\vec c_0=\frac{20-78+12}{7}=-\frac{46}{7}$ and $\vec m\cdot\vec s=10+3-8=5$.

useful_results: Component form of $\vec s\times\vec c$ for $\vec s=(s_1,s_2,s_3)$: $(s_2z-s_3y,\ s_3x-s_1z,\ s_1y-s_2x)$; its three equations are dependent, so a cross-product equation alone leaves a one-parameter family $\vec c_0+t\vec s$.
For $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ to have a solution, $\vec w\perp\vec s$ is necessary; check it as a free error test of your arithmetic ($70+10-80=0$ here).
$\vec a\times\vec b=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2-a_2b_1)$; verify $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec a,\vec b$ before using it.

concepts: Line meeting two given lines in 3D (collinearity of points)
questions.question: Let a line passing through the point $(-1,2,3)$ intersect the lines $L_1:\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z+1}{-2}$ at $M(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $L_2:\dfrac{x+2}{-3}=\dfrac{y-2}{-2}=\dfrac{z-1}{4}$ at $N(a,b,c)$. Then the value of $\dfrac{(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2}{(a+b+c)^2}$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: $P,M,N$ are collinear, so the direction ratios $\overrightarrow{PM}$ and $\overrightarrow{PN}$ are proportional.
solution: Let $P=(-1,2,3)$. A point of $L_1$ is $M(3\lambda+1,\,2\lambda+2,\,-2\lambda-1)$ and a point of $L_2$ is $N(-3\mu-2,\,-2\mu+2,\,4\mu+1)$.
The first two ratios give $\lambda=2\mu$; the last two then give $4\lambda\mu=4\lambda+8\mu$, i.e. $8\mu^2=16\mu$, so $\mu=2$ (the value $\mu=0$ makes the ratios meaningless).
questions.correction_note: The PDF jumps from the proportion of direction ratios to 'mu=2, lambda=4' without any working, and its final line 'alpha+beta+gamma = 14, a+b+c = -1' omits the points M and N. Added the elimination steps (lambda = 2 mu, then mu = 2) and the points M(13,10,-9), N(-8,-2,9). Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The required line lies in the plane through $P$ and $L_1$; it meets $L_2$ where $L_2$ pierces that plane.
solution: Plane through $P(-1,2,3)$ containing $L_1$: $L_1$ has point $(1,2,-1)$ and direction $(3,2,-2)$.
The line $PN$ has direction $(-7,-4,6)$ and meets $L_1$ at $M=P-2(-7,-4,6)=(13,10,-9)$, which satisfies $L_1$ (for $\lambda=4$).

useful_results: Transversal through a point $P$ meeting two skew lines $L_1,L_2$: it is the intersection of the plane $(P,L_1)$ with the plane $(P,L_2)$ - or find $N=L_2\cap(P,L_1)$ and join to $P$.
Three points are collinear iff their position differences are proportional: $\overrightarrow{PM}\times\overrightarrow{PN}=\vec0$.
A normal to the plane through a point $P$ and a line (point $Q$, direction $\vec d$) is $\vec d\times\overrightarrow{QP}$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point to a line in 3D
questions.question: Let $Q$ and $R$ be the feet of perpendiculars from the point $P(a,a,a)$ on the lines $x=y,\ z=1$ and $x=-y,\ z=-1$ respectively. If $\angle QPR$ is a right angle, then $12a^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Write each line in symmetric form, take its foot of the perpendicular, then impose $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF does not say that a=1 is degenerate: then Q=P (PQ is the zero vector) and the angle QPR is undefined, so only a=-1 gives a genuine right angle (P(-1,-1,-1), Q(-1,-1,1), R(0,0,-1)). Since a^2=1 either way, 12a^2=12 is unaffected. The two feet and the dot product are as in the PDF.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the feet by projecting $P$ within each plane $z=\pm1$ and apply Pythagoras $PQ^2+PR^2=QR^2$.
solution: $L_1$ lies in the plane $z=1$ along $y=x$: the foot of $(a,a,a)$ is $Q=(a,a,1)$ (the point $(a,a)$ is already on the line $x=y$).
$L_2$ lies in $z=-1$ along $y=-x$: the projection of $(a,a)$ on the line $y=-x$ is $(0,0)$ (since $(a,a)\perp(1,-1)$), so $R=(0,0,-1)$.

useful_results: The foot of the perpendicular from $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ to a line parallel to a coordinate plane (e.g. in the plane $z=k$) is found by projecting in that plane only: the $z$-coordinate is $k$.
$\angle QPR=90^\circ\iff\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=0\iff PQ^2+PR^2=QR^2$; also $P$ then lies on the sphere with $QR$ as diameter.
Always check a root for degeneracy: here $a=1$ gives $Q=P$, so the angle does not exist; the question still has the answer $12a^2=12$ from $a=-1$.

concepts: Equation of a line through two points and a point at a given distance on it
questions.question: A line passes through $A(4,-6,-2)$ and $B(16,-2,4)$. Then the point $P(a,b,c)$, where $a,b,c$ are non-negative integers, on the line $AB$ lies at a distance of $21$ units from the point $A$. The distance between the points $P(a,b,c)$ and $Q(4,-12,3)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Points at distance $d$ along a line are $A\pm d\hat u$; non-negative coordinates select the sign.
solution: Then $\dfrac{x-4}{6/7}=\dfrac{y+6}{2/7}=\dfrac{z+2}{3/7}=\pm21$ for a point at distance $21$ from $A$.
Taking $-21$ gives $(-14,-12,-11)$, which has negative coordinates, so it is rejected.
questions.correction_note: The PDF takes only the +21 point (x=22, y=0, z=7) without mentioning the other point at distance 21 on the line, (-14,-12,-11); it is the 'non-negative integers' condition that rules it out. Added that step. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $|\overrightarrow{QP}|^2=|\overrightarrow{QA}+21\hat u|^2$, so the coordinates of $P$ are never needed.
solution: $\hat u=\frac17(6,2,3)$ and, as above, $P=A+21\hat u$ (the sign is fixed by non-negativity, e.g. $y=-6+6=0$).

useful_results: Points at distance $d$ from $A$ on a line with direction ratios $(l,m,n)$ are $A\pm\dfrac{d}{\sqrt{l^2+m^2+n^2}}(l,m,n)$; here $\sqrt{36+4+9}=7$ is a perfect square root, so the points have integer coordinates.
$|\overrightarrow{QA}+d\hat u|^2=|QA|^2+2d\,\overrightarrow{QA}\cdot\hat u+d^2$ gives a distance from the moving point without its coordinates.
Integrality conditions (non-negative integers) are used to choose between the two points $A\pm d\hat u$.
